Stage 4 — DeepONet: the Darcy flow operator¶

Vamsi Gudipati

Instead of solving one field, I learn the map from a permeability field to its pressure field for steady Darcy flow. A finite-volume solver generates 1,500 training pairs on a 10×10 grid, a DeepONet (a branch for the input field, a trunk for the query point, joined by a dot product) learns the operator, and I score it on 80 held-out fields; Part B repeats it on a 16×16 grid. I ran the notebook's five closing experiments (more data or epochs, permeability contrast, number of basis functions, grid size, hand-drawn inputs outside the training family), added a training animation, and repeated every trained result with three seeds. deeponet_slide.py next to this notebook is a 40-line DeepONet for u'' = a on [0, 1].

Portfolio page: https://vamsigudipati.github.io/physics-informed-pinn-deeponet.html

Stage 4: DeepONet for Darcy Flow: Operator Learning Made Visible¶

Earlier sessions learned one solution at a time. A PINN trained on one boundary-value problem gives you that one field, change the coefficients and you retrain. This session learns a map between functions: give it a permeability field, get the pressure field back, with no solve and no retraining. That map is called an operator, and DeepONet is the gentlest way to learn one.

The problem. Steady Darcy flow through porous rock, the subsurface-flow workhorse:

$$-\nabla\cdot\big(a(x)\,\nabla u(x)\big)=f,\qquad u=0\ \text{on the boundary}.$$

The permeability $a(x)$ says how easily fluid moves through each point, the forcing $f=1$ is constant, and we solve for the pressure $u(x)$. We want the operator $G:a(\cdot)\mapsto u(\cdot)$: feed any permeability, read the pressure.

How DeepONet does it. Two small networks. The branch reads the input function (permeability sampled on a grid). The trunk reads a single query location $(x,y)$. Their outputs meet in a dot product. The formula $u(y)=\sum_k b_k(a)\,t_k(y)$ is a learned basis with input-dependent coefficients, a nonlinear cousin of a POD reconstruction.

# Heat-map of a field, with the value printed at each node on small grids.
# Copied from the Transolver companion so both notebooks read identically.
def plot_field(T, N, ax, title="", vmin=None, vmax=None, cmap="inferno", annot=None):
    g = np.asarray(T).reshape(N, N)
    vmin = g.min() if vmin is None else vmin
    vmax = g.max() if vmax is None else vmax
    im = ax.imshow(g, cmap=cmap, vmin=vmin, vmax=vmax)

    # Annotate each cell with its number (only when the grid is small enough).
    annot = (N <= 12) if annot is None else annot
    if annot:
        for r in range(N):
            for c in range(N):
                frac = (g[r, c] - vmin) / (vmax - vmin + 1e-9)
                label = f"{g[r,c]:.0f}" if abs(g[r,c]) >= 10 else f"{g[r,c]:.1f}"
                ax.text(c, r, label, ha="center", va="center",
                        color="white" if frac < 0.55 else "black",
                        fontsize=7 if N <= 10 else 5)

    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
    return im
In [6]:
# Three panels: reference | prediction | |error|, shared scale on the first two.
def compare(ref, pred, N, main=""):
    err = np.abs(pred - ref)
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11, 3.6))
    vmax = max(ref.max(), pred.max())

    plot_field(ref,  N, axs[0], "reference  u x1000", vmin=0, vmax=vmax)
    plot_field(pred, N, axs[1], "DeepONet  u x1000",  vmin=0, vmax=vmax)
    plot_field(err,  N, axs[2], f"|error| x1000 (max {err.max():.2f})",
               vmin=0, vmax=max(err.max(), 1e-9), cmap="viridis")

    fig.suptitle(main, fontsize=11); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Section 0. Warm-up: a family of solutions¶

Before any network, get concrete about what an operator is for. Take a thin rod of rock made of two materials: the left half has permeability $a_L$, the right half $a_R$. Push a constant forcing through it and solve 1D Darcy flow for the pressure $u(x)$. Two knobs go in, a whole curve comes out.

Turn the knobs and the curve changes. The map from $(a_L, a_R)$ to the pressure profile is a baby operator: two numbers to a function. A DeepONet does the same job with the two knobs replaced by the entire sampled field. That single change, from a couple of parameters to a whole function, is the step from ordinary regression to operator learning.

In [7]:
# 1D two-material Darcy: -(a u')' = f on [0,1], u(0)=u(1)=0.
# Face permeabilities are harmonic averages of the two neighbouring cells.
def darcy_1d(a_L, a_R, N=41, f=1.0):
    x = np.linspace(0, 1, N); h = x[1] - x[0]
    a = np.where(x < 0.5, a_L, a_R)
    harm = lambda p, q: 2*p*q/(p+q)

    # Assemble the tridiagonal system for the interior nodes.
    A = np.zeros((N-2, N-2)); b = np.full(N-2, f*h*h)
    for k in range(1, N-1):
        i = k-1
        aL = harm(a[k], a[k-1])
        aR = harm(a[k], a[k+1])
        A[i, i] = aL + aR
        if k-1 >= 1:   A[i, i-1] = -aL
        if k+1 <= N-2: A[i, i+1] = -aR

    u = np.zeros(N); u[1:-1] = np.linalg.solve(A, b)
    return x, u

Section 1. The reference solver¶

The pressure fields the DeepONet learns to reproduce come from a classical solve, not from the network. This is the finite-volume Darcy solver from the Transolver companion, copied unchanged: it discretises the unit square, averages permeability harmonically across each cell face, and solves the linear system. The permeability generator makes blocky two-material fields, the same distribution both notebooks train on.

In [9]:
# 2D finite-volume Darcy solver on the unit square, u = 0 on the boundary.
# Copied unchanged from the Transolver companion notebook.
def darcy_solve(a, f=1.0):
    N = a.shape[0]; h = 1.0/(N-1)

    # Index the interior nodes.
    inner = [(r, c) for r in range(1, N-1) for c in range(1, N-1)]
    pos = {rc: k for k, rc in enumerate(inner)}
    A = np.zeros((len(inner),)*2); b = np.zeros(len(inner))
    harm = lambda p, q: 2*p*q/(p+q)

    # One row per interior node: harmonic face weights to the four neighbours.
    for (r, c) in inner:
        k = pos[(r, c)]; b[k] = f*h*h; diag = 0
        for dr, dc in [(-1,0),(1,0),(0,-1),(0,1)]:
            rr, cc = r+dr, c+dc
            tw = harm(a[r, c], a[rr, cc]); diag += tw
            if (rr, cc) in pos:
                A[k, pos[(rr, cc)]] -= tw
        A[k, k] = diag

    # Solve and scatter the solution back onto the full grid.
    u = np.zeros((N, N)); sol = np.linalg.solve(A, b)
    for (r, c), k in pos.items():
        u[r, c] = sol[k]
    return u
In [10]:
# Blocky two-material permeability: a random coarse mask upsampled to N x N.
def random_perm(N, rng, hi=12.0, lo=3.0):
    nb = rng.integers(2, 5)                                  # blocks per axis
    cg = rng.random((nb, nb)) < rng.uniform(0.3, 0.7)        # random coarse mask
    a = np.kron(cg, np.ones((int(np.ceil(N/nb)),)*2))[:N, :N]
    return np.where(a, hi, lo)
In [11]:

plot_field(a,      N, axs[0], "permeability a(x)  (input)", cmap="cividis")
plot_field(u*1000, N, axs[1], "pressure u  x1000  (reference)")

Section 2. The DeepONet, one piece at a time¶

Two networks that never touch until the very end.

The branch reads the input function. We sample the permeability on the $N\times N$ grid and hand the branch all $m=N^2$ values at once. It returns a vector of $p$ numbers, one coefficient per basis function.

The trunk reads a location. Give it a single query point $(x,y)$ and it returns $p$ numbers, the value of each basis function at that point.

They meet in a dot product:

$$u(y)\;=\;\sum_{k=1}^{p} b_k(a)\,t_k(y)\;+\;b_0.$$

The trunk supplies spatial basis functions $t_k(y)$, and the branch supplies the coefficients $b_k$ that pick the right combination for this permeability. That is a POD reconstruction with both the modes and the coefficients learned, which is why the trunk outputs are worth a look later (Section 6).

Every sample lives on the same grid, so we evaluate the trunk once on all grid points and share it across the batch. The combine step becomes a single matrix product $B\,T^{\top}$.

In [13]:
# A small MLP with GELU activations and Xavier init, reused by both nets.
def mlp(d_in, width, depth, d_out, act=nn.GELU):
    layers = [nn.Linear(d_in, width), act()]
    for _ in range(depth-1):
        layers += [nn.Linear(width, width), act()]
    layers += [nn.Linear(width, d_out)]
    net = nn.Sequential(*layers)
    for m in net:
        if isinstance(m, nn.Linear):
            nn.init.xavier_normal_(m.weight); nn.init.zeros_(m.bias)
    return net
In [14]:
class DeepONet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, m_sensors, p=128, width=128, depth=3):
        super().__init__()
        self.branch = mlp(m_sensors, width, depth, p)   # field    -> p coefficients
        self.trunk  = mlp(2,         width, depth, p)   # location -> p basis values
        self.b0 = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1))

    def forward(self, a, y):
        B = self.branch(a)          # [batch, p]
        T = self.trunk(y)           # [n_query, p]
        return B @ T.T + self.b0    # [batch, n_query]

with torch.no_grad():
    B = demo.branch(a_batch)
    T = demo.trunk(y_grid)
    U = demo(a_batch, y_grid)

print("branch input  a :", tuple(a_batch.shape), "-> branch output b :", tuple(B.shape))
print("trunk  input  y :", tuple(y_grid.shape),  "-> trunk  output t :", tuple(T.shape))

Section 3. The dataset¶

One training example is a pair: a permeability field in, its reference pressure out. We generate many random fields, solve each one, and stack them. The branch input is the flattened permeability (scaled to roughly $[0,1]$), the trunk input is the fixed grid of query coordinates shared by every sample, and the target is the reference pressure (scaled to about $O(1)$ so training is well conditioned).

In [16]:
# Build a dataset of (permeability, pressure) pairs on the N x N grid.
def build_dataset(N, n, rng, hi=12.0, lo=3.0):
    xs = np.linspace(0, 1, N); XX, YY = np.meshgrid(xs, xs)
    coords = np.stack([XX.ravel(), YY.ravel()], -1).astype(np.float32)   # [N*N, 2]

    A = np.zeros((n, N*N), np.float32); U = np.zeros((n, N*N), np.float32)
    araw = np.zeros((n, N, N), np.float32)
    for i in range(n):
        a = random_perm(N, rng, hi, lo); u = darcy_solve(a)
        A[i] = ((a - lo)/(hi - lo)).ravel()      # branch input, scaled to ~[0,1]
        U[i] = u.ravel(); araw[i] = a
    return coords, A, U, araw
In [17]:
# Generate train and validation pairs, then scale and wrap as tensors.
NTRAIN, NVAL = 1500, 80
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
coords, Atr, Utr, Araw_tr = build_dataset(N, NTRAIN, rng)
coords_v, Ava, Uva, Araw_va = build_dataset(N, NVAL, rng)
uscale = float(Utr.max())                        # scale targets to ~O(1)

C   = torch.tensor(coords)                       # shared query grid  [N*N, 2]
At  = torch.tensor(Atr);   Ut  = torch.tensor(Utr/uscale)
Avt = torch.tensor(Ava);   Uvt = torch.tensor(Uva/uscale)

print("train:", At.shape[0], "| val:", Avt.shape[0],
      "| sensors/field:", At.shape[1], "| query points:", C.shape[0],
      "| uscale:", round(uscale, 5))

Section 4. Training¶

Standard supervised regression: minimise the mean squared error between predicted and reference pressure, with Adam and a cosine-decayed learning rate. We report the relative $L_2$ error on a held-out validation set, the usual accuracy number for PDE surrogates. This is the heaviest cell in the notebook and takes about a minute on a Colab CPU.

In [19]:
# Relative L2 error, the usual accuracy metric for PDE surrogates.
def rel_l2(pred, target):
    return (torch.norm(pred - target) / torch.norm(target)).item()
In [20]:
# Standard supervised training: Adam with a cosine-decayed learning rate.
def train_deeponet(model, At, Ut, C, epochs=200, bs=32, lr=2e-3, seed=0, log_every=40):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr)
    sched = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingLR(opt, epochs)
    lossf = nn.MSELoss(); hist = []

    for ep in range(1, epochs+1):
        model.train()
        perm = torch.randperm(len(At)); tot = 0.0; nb = 0

        # Mini-batch pass over the training pairs.
        for i in range(0, len(At), bs):
            b = perm[i:i+bs]; opt.zero_grad()
            loss = lossf(model(At[b], C), Ut[b])
            loss.backward(); opt.step()
            tot += loss.item(); nb += 1

        sched.step(); hist.append(tot/nb); ex_epoch_hook(model, ep, epochs, hist)  # hook: animation snapshot and checkpoint (main training only)
        if ep % log_every == 0 or ep == 1:
            print(f"  epoch {ep:3d} | train MSE {hist[-1]:.2e}")
    return hist

Training hook. train_deeponet calls ex_epoch_hook(model, ep, epochs, hist) at the end of every epoch. The hook is active only during the main training in the next cell and switches itself off when it ends, so Part B and the experiments are not recorded. Every 4 epochs it stores the training loss, the validation relative error and the prediction for validation field 0 for the training animation, and every 20 epochs it writes a checkpoint. It only evaluates the model under no_grad and draws no random numbers, so the training is unchanged.

In [21]:
from pathlib import Path
EX_CKPT = MODELS_DIR / "checkpoints"; EX_CKPT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
anim_snaps, EX_HOOK_ACTIVE = [], [True]
def ex_snap(model, ep, hist):
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        pred = model(Avt[0:1], C)[0].numpy() * uscale * 1000; err = rel_l2(model(Avt, C), Uvt)
    anim_snaps.append(dict(epoch=ep, pred=pred, val_err=err, loss=list(hist))); model.train()
def ex_epoch_hook(model, ep, epochs, hist):
    if not EX_HOOK_ACTIVE[0]: return
    if ep == 1 or ep % 4 == 0 or ep == epochs: ex_snap(model, ep, hist)
    if ep % 20 == 0 or ep == epochs: torch.save(model.state_dict(), EX_CKPT / f"deeponet_epoch{ep:03d}.pth")
    if ep == epochs: EX_HOOK_ACTIVE[0] = False

Section 5. Predicting unseen fields¶

The validation permeabilities were never used in training. For each one the DeepONet produces the pressure field in a single forward pass, no linear system and no iteration. The triptych shows the reference, the prediction, and the absolute error on the same colour scale.

The throughput line times the same fields both ways. On this tiny grid the classical solve is already fast per field, so the point is not a headline speedup here, it is that the network answers a whole batch in one shot, and that gap widens as the grid grows and as you need thousands of evaluations (design sweeps, inversion, uncertainty quantification).

In [24]:
# Predict three held-out fields and show the error maps.
for smp in [0, 1, 2]:
    with torch.no_grad():
        pred = model(Avt[smp:smp+1], C)[0].numpy() * uscale * 1000
    ref = Uva[smp] * 1000
    compare(ref, pred, N, main=f"unseen field {smp}: DeepONet vs reference")
    print(f"  field {smp}: relative L2 =",
          round(float(np.linalg.norm(pred-ref) / np.linalg.norm(ref)), 4))

# Throughput: classical solve (one field at a time) vs one batched forward pass.
K = Avt.shape[0]
t0 = time.time()
for _ in range(K):
    darcy_solve(random_perm(N, rng))
solver_s = time.time() - t0

with torch.no_grad():
    t0 = time.time(); _ = model(Avt, C); net_s = time.time() - t0

print(f"\n{K} fields:  solver {solver_s*1000:.0f} ms ({solver_s/K*1000:.2f} ms/field)"

Section 6. What the trunk learned¶

The prediction is a weighted sum of trunk basis functions, so the trunk outputs are worth seeing. Each of the $p$ trunk channels is a scalar function over the grid, and a handful are plotted below. They are not the clean, ranked, orthogonal modes of a POD (nothing forces that here), but together they span the space the pressures live in, and the branch chooses the weights. This is the concrete meaning of "combine by dot product".

In [25]:
# The learned basis: a few trunk channels as fields over the grid.
with torch.no_grad():
    Tbasis = model.trunk(C).numpy()          # [N*N, p]

show = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, len(show), figsize=(2.3*len(show), 2.6))
for j, k in enumerate(show):
    plot_field(Tbasis[:, k], N, axs[j], f"trunk basis {k}", cmap="magma", annot=False)
fig.suptitle("a handful of the p learned basis functions  t_k(x, y)", y=1.04)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
In [26]:
# The branch turns one permeability into the coefficients that weight this basis.
with torch.no_grad():
    coeffs = model.branch(Avt[0:1])[0].numpy()

print("for validation field 0, branch coefficients b_k:")
print("  shape", coeffs.shape, "| min %.2f  max %.2f  (p = %d basis functions)"
      % (coeffs.min(), coeffs.max(), len(coeffs)))

Part B: a finer grid, and a limitation worth knowing¶

Rerun the whole pipeline at $N=16$. The solver, the data builder, the model class, and the training loop are all unchanged. One thing does change, and it matters: the branch now reads $16^2=256$ sensor values instead of $100$. The branch input width is baked into the architecture, so the coarse-grid model cannot accept the finer field. We build a fresh model and train it.

That is the honest limitation of the plain DeepONet: it is tied to the sensor layout it was trained on. Change the grid and you change the branch. The operator families in Section 7 are built to relax this.

In [27]:
# Part B: rerun the whole pipeline at N = 16, nothing else changes.
Nb = 16
rng_b = np.random.default_rng(2)
coords_b,  Atr_b, Utr_b, Araw_b  = build_dataset(Nb, 1000, rng_b)
coords_bv, Ava_b, Uva_b, Araw_bv = build_dataset(Nb, 60,   rng_b)
uscale_b = float(Utr_b.max())

Cb   = torch.tensor(coords_b)
Atb  = torch.tensor(Atr_b);  Utb  = torch.tensor(Utr_b/uscale_b)
Avtb = torch.tensor(Ava_b);  Uvtb = torch.tensor(Uva_b/uscale_b)
In [28]:
# The branch input width is baked in: N=16 gives 256 sensors, not 100.
print(f"N={Nb}: {Nb*Nb} sensors/field, {Nb*Nb} query points")

# So the coarse (N=10) model cannot read a 256-value field.
try:
    _ = model.branch(Atb[:1])
except RuntimeError as e:
    print("coarse-grid branch on a 256-value field ->", str(e).split(".")[0])

Section 7. Where DeepONet sits¶

DeepONet is one operator family. Two others come up constantly, and the choice between them is mostly about the mesh.

Method Reads the field as Reach for it when
DeepONet values at fixed sensors, plus query points you want a gentle, general default that just works
FNO a regular grid, filtered in Fourier space the data lives on a clean uniform grid
Transolver an unordered set of points the geometry is messy: unstructured meshes, point clouds, changing resolution

The one-line rule: regular grid, reach for FNO. Messy geometry or a point cloud, reach for Transolver. Unsure, start with DeepONet. The Transolver notebook is a separate demo on this same Darcy problem, so you can put the two side by side.

Takeaways¶

  • An operator maps a whole function to a whole function. Train once on many solved cases, then predict the field for a new input in a single forward pass. No resolve, no retrain.
  • Branch and trunk split the job. The branch reads what the input is (the permeability), the trunk reads where you are asking (a location), and a dot product combines them. The formula $u=\sum_k b_k(a)\,t_k(y)$ is a learned basis with input-dependent coefficients.
  • It is ordinary supervised learning underneath. Solved cases from a classical solver, MSE loss, Adam. The operator idea lives in the architecture, not the training.
  • The plain DeepONet is tied to its sensor grid. Changing resolution means a new branch. That constraint is exactly what FNO and Transolver are built to loosen.

Experiment: change this and rerun¶

  • Raise NTRAIN or EPOCHS and watch the validation error drop. Both notebooks are trained deliberately light.
  • Change the permeability contrast in random_perm (hi, lo) and see whether sharper materials are harder to learn.
  • Change p, the number of basis functions, and see how few the trunk really needs.
  • Set a different grid N. The branch width must match, so build a fresh model whenever N changes.
  • Feed the trained model a permeability you draw by hand (a single block, a smooth gradient) and see how it behaves outside the training distribution.

My runs of the five experiments¶

I ran the five experiments of the closing section with the notebook's own solver (darcy_solve, random_perm, build_dataset), model (DeepONet), training function (train_deeponet, Adam with cosine decay, batch 32, learning rate 2e-3) and metric (rel_l2). Every variant is trained from scratch with seed 0 and scored by the relative $\ell_2$ error on its own validation fields, on the CPU like the rest of the notebook. I kept each experiment to at most three new settings, eleven trainings in all. The notebook's own configuration is not retrained: its row is the model trained above, marked "base model" and scored on the notebook's validation fields.

In [31]:
import pandas as pd
from pathlib import Path
ex_dir = EXERCISES_DIR; ex_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
def ex_run(Ngrid=N, ntrain=NTRAIN, nval=NVAL, epochs=EPOCHS, p=128, hi=12.0, lo=3.0, seed=1):
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    co, A_, U_, _ = build_dataset(Ngrid, ntrain, r, hi, lo); _, Av_, Uv_, _ = build_dataset(Ngrid, nval, r, hi, lo)
    us = float(U_.max()); Ct = torch.tensor(co)
    m = DeepONet(m_sensors=Ngrid * Ngrid, p=p, width=128, depth=3); t0 = time.time()
    h = train_deeponet(m, torch.tensor(A_), torch.tensor(U_ / us), Ct, epochs=epochs, bs=32, lr=2e-3, log_every=10**9)
    m.eval()
    with torch.no_grad(): err = rel_l2(m(torch.tensor(Av_), Ct), torch.tensor(Uv_ / us))
    return dict(val_rel_l2=err, final_train_mse=h[-1], train_s=round(time.time() - t0))
with torch.no_grad(): ex_base_err = rel_l2(model(Avt, C), Uvt)
ex_base_row = dict(val_rel_l2=ex_base_err, final_train_mse=hist[-1], train_s=None, source="base model")
print(f"base model: validation relative L2 = {ex_base_err:.4f}")

base model: validation relative L2 = 0.0520

Experiment 5 — hand-drawn permeabilities¶

I feed the trained base model four permeabilities drawn by hand on its 10×10 grid: a single high-permeability block in a low background, a smooth left-to-right gradient from 3 to 12 (not two-valued, so outside the training distribution), a checkerboard of single cells (finer than any training block), and a uniform field. Each is compared with the reference solution.

In [36]:
def ex_hand(name):
    a = np.full((N, N), 3.0)
    if name == "single block": a[3:7, 3:7] = 12.0
    elif name == "smooth gradient": a = np.tile(np.linspace(3.0, 12.0, N), (N, 1))
    elif name == "checkerboard": a = np.where((np.add.outer(np.arange(N), np.arange(N)) % 2) == 0, 12.0, 3.0)
    elif name == "uniform 12": a[:] = 12.0
    return a
ex5_rows = []; fig, axs5 = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(15, 6.5))
for j, name in enumerate(("single block", "smooth gradient", "checkerboard", "uniform 12")):
    a = ex_hand(name); u = darcy_solve(a)
    with torch.no_grad(): pr = model(torch.tensor(((a - 3.0) / 9.0).ravel()[None], dtype=torch.float32), C)[0].numpy() * uscale
    ex5_rows.append(dict(permeability=name, rel_l2=float(np.linalg.norm(pr - u.ravel()) / np.linalg.norm(u)), u_max_ref=float(u.max()), u_max_pred=float(pr.max())))
    plot_field(u * 1000, N, axs5[0, j], f"{name}: reference x1000", annot=False); plot_field(pr * 1000, N, axs5[1, j], "DeepONet x1000", vmin=0, vmax=u.max() * 1000, annot=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig(ex_dir / "exp5_hand_drawn.png", dpi=100); plt.show()
ex5 = pd.DataFrame(ex5_rows); ex5.to_csv(ex_dir / "exp5_hand_drawn.csv", index=False); print(ex5)
print("Result (Experiment 5): relative L2 of the base model " + "; ".join(f"{r.permeability}: {r.rel_l2:.3f}" for r in ex5.itertuples()) + f" (validation fields: {ex_base_err:.3f})")

Three seeds¶

I repeat every trained result above with the seeds 0, 1 and 2. The main configuration (1,500 fields, 200 epochs, p = 128, 10×10 grid) and the 16×16 model of Part B are retrained on the same data with the training seed changed (seed 0 is the run above). The five experiments use ex_run_s, a copy of ex_run in which the seed drives both the data draw (default_rng(1 + seed), so seed 0 uses the same data as the experiments above) and the training (train_deeponet(seed=seed)). Each row is one training run; the summaries give the mean and the standard deviation over the three seeds. Tables and figure: ../results/04_deeponet_darcy_operator/exercises/; seed models of the main configuration: ../models/04_deeponet_darcy_operator/.

Experiments 1 to 4 with three seeds¶

In [40]:
def ex_run_s(seed, Ngrid=N, ntrain=NTRAIN, nval=NVAL, epochs=EPOCHS, p=128, hi=12.0, lo=3.0):
    r = np.random.default_rng(1 + seed)
    co, A_, U_, _ = build_dataset(Ngrid, ntrain, r, hi, lo); _, Av_, Uv_, _ = build_dataset(Ngrid, nval, r, hi, lo)
    us = float(U_.max()); Ct = torch.tensor(co)
    m = DeepONet(m_sensors=Ngrid * Ngrid, p=p, width=128, depth=3); t0 = time.time()
    h = train_deeponet(m, torch.tensor(A_), torch.tensor(U_ / us), Ct, epochs=epochs, bs=32, lr=2e-3, seed=seed, log_every=10**9)
    m.eval()
    with torch.no_grad(): err = rel_l2(m(torch.tensor(Av_), Ct), torch.tensor(Uv_ / us))
    return dict(val_rel_l2=err, final_train_mse=h[-1], train_s=round(time.time() - t0))
rows_e = []
for s in SEEDS:
    for nt_, ep_ in ((500, 200), (1500, 200), (3000, 200), (1500, 100)):
        rows_e.append(dict(experiment="1 data and epochs", setting=f"{nt_} fields x {ep_} epochs", seed=s, **ex_run_s(s, ntrain=nt_, epochs=ep_)))
    print(f"seed {s}: experiment 1 done")
seeds_e1 = pd.DataFrame(rows_e); seeds_e1.to_csv(ex_dir / "seeds_exp1_runs.csv", index=False); print(seeds_e1.round(5).to_string())
